example.reason: The two aces make a pair. Fill the remaining three places with king, queen and nine. Your private six and the shared two are left out. The six is not required just because it was dealt privately to you.

cases.title: A pair still needs three side cards
cases.prompt: Choose the strongest five cards available on this completed board. Say which two you leave out and why.
cases.hint: After making your pair, fill all three remaining places with the highest available side cards.
cases.reason: Use both aces, then king, queen and nine. The six and two do not belong in the strongest five. This selection uses both private cards.

cases.title: Five cards without a pair
cases.prompt: None of these seven cards makes a pair, straight or flush. Build the strongest five, rather than stopping at the highest single card.
cases.hint: High-card hands still contain five cards. Put the ranks in order and remove the two lowest.
cases.reason: A-K-Q-9-8 is the strongest five. The six and two are excluded. Every one of the five ranks can matter when otherwise equal high-card hands are compared.

cases.title: Your original pocket pair changes roles
cases.prompt: The board has two pairs. Choose your best five. Either physical card is acceptable when two choices have the same rank and make equally strong hands.
cases.hint: Choose the two highest pairs first. There is room for only one side card after those four cards.
cases.reason: A-A-K-K-T is best. The tens are no longer one of the two pairs in your best five. Either your ten of spades or your ten of hearts can fill the final place; both selections are equally strong. This hand uses one private card.

cases.title: Keep all three matching cards
cases.prompt: Build your best five on this completed board. The two higher single cards do not erase a matching group.
cases.hint: Find the three matching ranks, then choose the two highest remaining side cards.
cases.reason: Three fives with ace and king is strongest: 5-5-5-A-K. Keeping only two fives would discard the stronger made hand. Both private cards play.

cases.title: Leave both private cards out
cases.prompt: Use any five of the seven available cards. There is no requirement to include a private card.
cases.hint: Look for five consecutive ranks on the shared board before adding a private card.
cases.reason: K-Q-J-T-9 is a king-high straight entirely on the board. Neither private card improves it. A sixth card cannot improve an otherwise identical five-card hand; another remaining player who also cannot improve this board would tie.

cases.title: One private diamond is enough
cases.prompt: Choose the strongest five, using exactly the cards shown. The number of private cards used is a result of the selection, not a fixed rule.
cases.hint: Count all available diamonds. A flush needs five cards of one suit and does not require two private cards.
cases.reason: A-Q-T-8-5 of diamonds is an ace-high flush. Your queen joins the four shared diamonds. The four of spades and two of hearts are left out, so only one private card plays.

cases.title: Two matching groups fit together
cases.prompt: Choose five cards, then name the matching groups in the hand you built.
cases.hint: Three equal ranks together with a different pair form a full house. Compare that category with two pair or three of a kind.
cases.reason: 8-8-8-K-K is a full house, eights full of kings. The three eights supply the three-of-a-kind group and the two kings supply the pair. The two and three are excluded.

cases.title: The side card still matters
cases.prompt: Four matching cards are shared. Choose the fifth card as well; do not stop at naming the group.
cases.hint: After using all four nines, choose the highest remaining side card.
cases.reason: 9-9-9-9-A is strongest. The ace is the kicker; your three and the shared two are lower. A player's kicker can distinguish hands when the same four of a kind is on the board.

cases.title: Two patterns in the same five cards
cases.prompt: Build the strongest five, then explain how both rank order and suits describe the same selection.
cases.hint: Look for five consecutive ranks that also share one suit. A single high king does not replace a card in that pattern.
cases.reason: 8-7-6-5-4 of hearts is an eight-high straight flush. Both private cards play. A royal flush is the ace-high version of this category, not a requirement for every straight flush.

cases.title: An ace can complete the low end
cases.prompt: Choose the strongest five. Decide whether to keep the pair on the board or build another category.
cases.hint: A-2-3-4-5 is a valid five-high straight. The ace acts below the two in this sequence; it cannot wrap through K-A-2-3-4.
cases.reason: 5-4-3-2-A is a five-high straight and beats the available pair of kings. Both private cards play. The ace does not make this an ace-high straight or supply an extra high-card tiebreaker.
